  This whitepaper documents the automated extraction pipeline of the Sustainability Reporting Navigator (SRN). The SRN
  extracts two dimensions, a Transparency dimension and an environmental, social and governance (ESG) dimension. The
  Transparency dimension captures textual characteristics such as length and readibility as well as
  environmental and social topic shares. The ESG dimension retrieves and extracts predefined sets of ESG
  indicators from firms' annual and sustainability reports using a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based approach.

# Introduction

The Sustainability Reporting Navigator (SRN) provides structured, machine-readable datasets on corporate sustainability
reporting, built by automatically processing firms' annual and sustainability reports. The underlying pipeline addresses
two complementary questions: how firms report, and what they report. The first is captured by a set of transparency
dimensions: textual characteristics such as length, readability, and tone, together with the share of disclosure devoted
to environmental and social topics as defined by the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). The second is
captured by predefined set of data points, retrieved and extracted from the source documents using a artifical
intelligence pipeline.

This document provides the technical documentation. It is intended for researchers and practitioners who wish to understand how the data was produced, assess its reliability, and use it correctly in downstream analysis.

# Methodology
This chapter describes the methodology underlying the SRN's extraction pipeline. We first document how the SRN extracts the **Transparency** dimensions from firms' annual and sustainability reports (Section [Transparency]), then describe how the SRN extracts a predefined set of **quantitative ESG indicators** (Section [Extraction Pipeline]).

## Transparency

The transparency dimensions captured by the SRN dataset describe **how** firms report. To that end, we capture
textual characteristics (e.g., length and readability) and environmental and social topic shares. The corporate reports are first
parsed with Docling [@docling2024] and then processed with Python at the sentence level. The language model used to
classify passages into environmental and social topics was originally developed for @Donau2024-yc. We adopt their label
set and decision thresholds without modification, and refer the reader to that paper for full methodological detail.

In what follows we summarise the two transparency dimensions exposed through the dashboard: a set of report-level textual characteristics (Section [Textual characteristics]) and a sentence-level classifier that locates passages addressing environmental and social topics (Section [Environmental and social topics]).

### Textual characteristics

For each (firm, year, report) we compute a set of report-level features describing the document's overall structure and writing style. They are stored alongside the extracted ESG indicators and exposed in the API as a single row per report under the `transparency` field. The features fall into three groups:

- **Length and structure.** Total word count (`total_words`), page count (`pages`), and the number of tables (`total_tables`). `image_ratio` is the share of pages that contain at least one image.

- **Readability.** `reading_difficulty` is the mean Gunning Fog index computed at the sentence level and averaged over the document. Higher values indicate more complex prose. `tone` is a sentiment ratio $(w^{+} - w^{-})/(w^{+} + w^{-})$, where $w^{+}$ and $w^{-}$ are the counts of positive and negative words from the @Loughran2011 financial-sentiment dictionary; the ratio is set to zero when both counts are zero. `numbers` is the density of numerical tokens, defined as total numeric tokens divided by total words.


### Environmental and social topics

We conduct the topic classification at the sentence level to capture the share of text devoted to different environmental and social topics. 
We tag each parsed sentence with one or more topic labels covering the environmental and social pillars of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards. The classifier is the supervised model (ESRS Bert) trained in @Donau2024-yc. Its output is a long table with one row per (document, sentence) carrying the predicted label(s), the model's confidence score, and the original page number.

The classifier covers nine topic labels aligned with the topical ESRS standards: five environmental — *E1 Climate Change*, *E2 Pollution*, *E3 Water and Marine Resources*, *E4 Biodiversity and Ecosystems*, and *E5 Resource Use and Circular Economy* — and four social — *S1 Own Workforce*, *S2 Workers in the Value Chain*, *S3 Affected Communities*, and *S4 Consumers and End-Users*. 

For each topic, we report the share of sentences in the sustainability statement assigned to that label, aggregated across all sentences classified as ES-relevant by the model. A sentence is attributed to a topic when the model's confidence score exceeds the decision threshold selected during validation.

The training corpus consists of more than 13,500 manually labelled pages drawn from 200 randomly selected annual and sustainability reports (2023–2024). Page-level labels were refined at the sentence level using GPT-5-nano, and the resulting data were used to fine-tune RoBERTa. Comprehensive classifier statistics, e.g.,  accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score by topic  will be reported in the final published version of @Donau2024-yc. `\hyperref[tab:transparency]{Table~\ref{tab:transparency}}`{=latex} displays all transparency dimensions stored in the `transparency` array.

## Extraction Pipeline
This section documents how the SRN extracts the **quantitative** ESG indicators from firms' annual and sustainability reports and how accurately it does so. We first introduce the list of indicators currently in scope (Section [Data Point Packages]) and the rationale for the selection, then walk through the extraction pipeline end-to-end (Section [Pipeline setup]), report its accuracy on a human-reviewed subset of the most recent public release (Section [Pipeline performance]).

### Data Point Packages
The SRN defines sets of data points that are extracted from firms' annual and sustainability reports. Each datapoint is defined by a name, a unit of measurement, and a precise definition that specifies what to extract and what to ignore. 

All inputs underlying the figures and tables of this document are publicly available. Refer to the Chapter [Working with
the Data] for details on how to access the data.

\columnbreak

#### Main ESRS KPI dataset
The *Main ESRS KPI dataset* covers all three ESG dimensions and is rooted in the European Sustainability Reporting
Standards (ESRS, as prescribed by the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive).
`\hyperref[tab:indicators]{Table~\ref{tab:indicators}}`{=latex} shows the datapoints currently included in the *Main
ESRS KPI dataset*. The full definitions are provided in the Section [Data Point Package Definition Guide] in the Appendix.

```{python}
#| label: data-acquisition-setup
#| echo: false
#| output: false

import json, re, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

# === Choose the release version here. ===

RELEASE      = "v2.4"

# ========================================

BASE         = f"https://lab.srnav.com/p/main-esrs-kpi/{RELEASE}"
RELEASE_JSON = Path(f"release_{RELEASE.replace('.', '_')}.json")
SNAPSHOT     = Path(f"performance_snapshot_{RELEASE.replace('.', '_')}.json")

# Datapoints added to the package that are out of scope for this whitepaper.
EXCLUDED_FIELD_SLUGS = {"revenues", "currency"}

def _http_get(url: str) -> bytes:
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "srn-whitepaper/1.0"})
    return urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30).read()

def _balanced(text: str, start: int) -> str:
    depth, in_str, q, esc = 0, False, None, False
    for i in range(start, len(text)):
        c = text[i]
        if in_str:
            if   esc:        esc = False
            elif c == "\\":  esc = True
            elif c == q:     in_str = False
        else:
            if   c in ('"', "'"): in_str, q = True, c
            elif c == "{":         depth += 1
            elif c == "}":
                depth -= 1
                if depth == 0:
                    return text[start: i + 1]
    raise RuntimeError("unbalanced braces")

if not RELEASE_JSON.exists():
    RELEASE_JSON.write_bytes(_http_get(f"{BASE}/data.json"))

if not SNAPSHOT.exists():
    html   = _http_get(BASE).decode("utf-8")
    anchor = html.find("performance:{")
    if anchor == -1:
        raise RuntimeError("performance snapshot not found on release page")
    js   = _balanced(html, html.find("{", anchor))
    text = re.sub(r"([{,])([A-Za-z_]\w*):", r'\1"\2":', js)
    SNAPSHOT.write_text(json.dumps(json.loads(text), indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
```

```{python}
# Release facts (version, company count, publication date) read straight out
# of the fetched release JSON, so prose mentions below stay in sync with
# whatever release RELEASE actually points to.

_release_data = json.loads(RELEASE_JSON.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_release_meta = _release_data["release"]

RELEASE_VERSION_STR   = f"v{_release_meta['version_number']}.{_release_meta['version_minor']}"

# split "." out: pandoc mis-escapes it to \. (LaTeX dot-accent) inside \texttt{}
RELEASE_VERSION_MAJOR = f"v{_release_meta['version_number']}"
RELEASE_VERSION_MINOR = str(_release_meta['version_minor'])

RELEASE_COMPANY_COUNT = len(_release_data["companies"])
RELEASE_DATE          = _release_meta["published_at"][:10]
```

```{python}
#| label: performance-metadata
#| echo: false
#| output: false

# Evaluation stats (pair counts, accuracy, per-category accuracy) read
# straight out of the fetched performance snapshot, so the "Pipeline
# Performance" prose below stays in sync with whatever the snapshot says.

_perf_snapshot = json.loads(SNAPSHOT.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_perf_snapshot["by_field"] = [
    r for r in _perf_snapshot["by_field"] if r["field_slug"] not in EXCLUDED_FIELD_SLUGS
]

_perf_totals = {
    k: sum(r[k] for r in _perf_snapshot["by_field"])
    for k in ("correct", "wrong", "fn", "fp", "error", "reviewed_total", "pending_total")
}
_perf_totals["accuracy_pct"] = round(100 * _perf_totals["correct"] / _perf_totals["reviewed_total"])

PERF_TOTAL_FMT   = f"{_perf_totals['reviewed_total']:,}"
PERF_CORRECT_FMT = f"{_perf_totals['correct']:,}"
PERF_ACCURACY    = _perf_totals["accuracy_pct"]

PERF_WRONG_FMT = f"{_perf_totals['wrong']:,}"
PERF_WRONG_PCT = round(100 * _perf_totals["wrong"] / _perf_totals["reviewed_total"])
PERF_FN_FMT    = f"{_perf_totals['fn']:,}"
PERF_FN_PCT    = round(100 * _perf_totals["fn"] / _perf_totals["reviewed_total"])
PERF_FP_FMT    = f"{_perf_totals['fp']:,}"
PERF_FP_PCT    = round(100 * _perf_totals["fp"] / _perf_totals["reviewed_total"])
PERF_ERROR_FMT = f"{_perf_totals['error']:,}"
PERF_ERROR_PCT = round(100 * _perf_totals["error"] / _perf_totals["reviewed_total"])

_perf_by_category = {}
for _row in _perf_snapshot["by_field"]:
    _agg = _perf_by_category.setdefault(_row["category"], {"correct": 0, "total": 0})
    _agg["correct"] += _row["correct"]
    _agg["total"]   += _row["reviewed_total"]

_perf_acc_social_str = f"{100 * _perf_by_category['social']['correct'] / _perf_by_category['social']['total']:.1f}"
_perf_acc_env_str    = f"{100 * _perf_by_category['environmental']['correct'] / _perf_by_category['environmental']['total']:.1f}"
# split "." out: pandoc mis-escapes it to \. (LaTeX dot-accent) otherwise
PERF_ACC_SOCIAL_INT, PERF_ACC_SOCIAL_DEC = _perf_acc_social_str.split(".")
PERF_ACC_ENV_INT, PERF_ACC_ENV_DEC       = _perf_acc_env_str.split(".")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import json, pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

# Indicator schema: prefer the richer local CSV (carries the ESRS reference
# code), fall back to the public release JSON.
csv_path = Path(f"schema_fields_rows_{RELEASE.replace('.', '_')}.csv")
if csv_path.exists():
    df = (
        pd.read_csv(csv_path)
          .query("is_active == True")
          .sort_values(["category", "display_order"])
          .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    show_ref = True
else:
    fields = json.loads(Path(f"release_{RELEASE.replace('.', '_')}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["fields"]
    df = (
        pd.DataFrame(fields)
          .sort_values(["category", "display_order"])
          .reset_index(drop=True)
    )
    df["reference"] = ""  # not exposed in the public release feed
    show_ref = False

df = df[~df["slug"].isin(EXCLUDED_FIELD_SLUGS)].reset_index(drop=True)

category_meta = {
    "environmental": "Environmental",
    "social":        "Social",
    "governance":    "Governance",
}

def esc(s):
    if s is None or (isinstance(s, float) and pd.isna(s)):
        return ""
    repl = {"&": r"\&", "%": r"\%", "$": r"\$", "#": r"\#",
            "_": r"\_", "{": r"\{", "}": r"\}",
            "~": r"\textasciitilde{}", "^": r"\textasciicircum{}"}
    return "".join(repl.get(c, c) for c in str(s))

tabular_spec = "@{}l l l@{}" if show_ref else "@{}l l@{}"
ncols        = 3 if show_ref else 2
header       = (r"\textbf{Ref.} & \textbf{Indicator} & \textbf{Unit} \\"
                if show_ref else
                r"\textbf{Indicator} & \textbf{Unit} \\")

out = [
    r"\begin{table}[H]",
    r"\centering\footnotesize",
    r"\setlength{\tabcolsep}{6pt}",
    r"\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.05}",
    r"\caption{ESG indicators extracted by the pipeline.}",
    r"\label{tab:indicators}",
    rf"\begin{{tabular}}{{{tabular_spec}}}",
    r"\toprule",
    header,
    r"\midrule",
]

for i, cat in enumerate(["environmental", "social", "governance"]):
    if i > 0:
        out.append(r"\addlinespace[2pt]\midrule")
    out.append(rf"\multicolumn{{{ncols}}}{{@{{}}l}}{{\textit{{{category_meta[cat]}}}}} \\")
    out.append(r"\addlinespace[2pt]")
    for _, row in df[df["category"] == cat].iterrows():
        name = esc(row["name"]).capitalize()
        unit = esc(row["unit"]) if pd.notna(row["unit"]) and str(row["unit"]).strip() else "—"
        if show_ref:
            ref = esc(row["reference"])
            out.append(rf"{ref} & {name} & {unit} \\")
        else:
            out.append(rf"{name} & {unit} \\")

out += [
    r"\bottomrule",
    r"\end{tabular}",
    r"\end{table}",
]

print("\n".join(out))
```

### Pipeline Setup

Our extraction pipeline builds on the design described by @forster2026. For each firm-year, we extract a predefined 
set of ESG indicators from the firm's annual report and sustainability report. 
Figure \ref{fig:pipeline} summarises the pipeline end-to-end.

The pipeline consists of multiple steps that can be grouped into two lanes: a one-off indexing lane that runs once per
document, and a per-indicator extraction lane that runs once for each indicator. 

The indexing lane prepares the source documents for retrieval. It first parses the documents with Docling
[@docling2024] to extract text, tables, and figures, then splits the text into overlapping chunks of roughly
1,000 characters with a 200-character overlap. Each chunk is embedded into a vector representation using
Mistral's text embedding model `mistral-embed-2312` [@mistralembed2023] and stored in a `pgvector` cosine-similarity
index. This index allows for efficient retrieval of relevant chunks during the extraction phase.

The extraction lane extracts the value of each indicator from the indexed chunks. For each indicator, Mistral's
language model `mistral-large-2513` [@mistrallarge2025] generates a natural-language query based on the indicator's
definition, embeds the query, and
retrieves the top five relevant chunks using a hybrid retrieval strategy that combines vector similarity with BM25
lexical scoring. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) is used to merge the two ranked lists, with weights of $0.7$ for the
vector channel and $0.3$ for the lexical channel. A cosine-similarity floor of $0.70$ is applied to filter out less
relevant chunks. The retrieved chunks, together with a custom prompt and a structured output schema, are passed to
Mistral's language model `mistral-large-2513` [@mistrallarge2025]. The prompt specifies the indicator definition,
the expected unit of measurement, and instructions
for handling absent disclosures. The model returns the extracted value, its source page, a confidence score in
$[0,1]$, and a short justification. Outputs are validated in-flight against a Zod schema; responses that violate
the schema are discarded and logged rather than retried, to avoid propagating model errors downstream.
If a response is well-formed but reports that the answer is present in the retrieved sources yet could not be
extracted as a clean value, the query is reformulated by the model and retrieval is repeated, up to three times in total.
All indicators per firm-year are extracted in batches of five and results are written to a relational table 
with one row per indicator–firm–year triplet. Each record retains the source-document identifier and page number, 
enabling manual verification against the original filing.


```{=latex}
\begin{multicols}{2}
```

# Pipeline Performance

The systematic extraction allows for a quantiative assessment of the pipeline's performance. We evaluate every 
AI-extracted value against a human-verified ground truth.


## Main ESRS KPI dataset

 The evaluation set used for the *Main ESRS KPI* dataset is the human-reviewed subset of public release \texttt{`{python} RELEASE_VERSION_MAJOR`.`{python} RELEASE_VERSION_MINOR`}, covering `{python} PERF_TOTAL_FMT` firm--indicator--year pairs for Euro Stoxx 50 and DAX 40 companies in the reporting years 2024 and 2025. Each pair was independently inspected by a trained reviewer who either accepted the AI's output, replaced it with the correct number, or marked the indicator as not disclosed. Outcomes are partitioned into five mutually exclusive classes: \emph{correct} (the AI value matches the reviewer's value, including agreement on non-disclosure); \emph{wrong} (both the AI and the reviewer extracted a number but the values disagree); \emph{false negative} (the AI returned \texttt{NOT\_FOUND} but the reviewer found a value); \emph{false positive} (the AI returned a value but the reviewer marked the indicator as not disclosed); and \emph{schema error} (the AI's structured output failed Zod validation). @fig-performance reports the per-indicator breakdown of these outcomes, sorted by accuracy.

Aggregated across all 25 indicators, the pipeline reaches an accuracy of $`{python} PERF_ACCURACY`\%$ on the reviewed subset (`{python} PERF_CORRECT_FMT` of `{python} PERF_TOTAL_FMT` pairs). Breaking this down by category, governance (one indicator) and social ($`{python} PERF_ACC_SOCIAL_INT`.`{python} PERF_ACC_SOCIAL_DEC`\%$) lie slightly above this mean while environmental indicators ($`{python} PERF_ACC_ENV_INT`.`{python} PERF_ACC_ENV_DEC`\%$) lie slightly below it, driven primarily by the harder Scope 1--3 greenhouse-gas emissions. Across error modes, \emph{wrong} extractions (`{python} PERF_WRONG_FMT` pairs, $`{python} PERF_WRONG_PCT`\%$ of the reviewed set) are the largest single failure class, followed by \emph{false negatives} (`{python} PERF_FN_FMT` pairs, $`{python} PERF_FN_PCT`\%$); \emph{false positives} (`{python} PERF_FP_FMT`, $`{python} PERF_FP_PCT`\%$) and \emph{schema errors} (`{python} PERF_ERROR_FMT`, $`{python} PERF_ERROR_PCT`\%$) are comparatively rare.

False negatives concentrate on the greenhouse-gas indicators (Scope 1, Scope 2 location- and market-based, total emissions, and Scope 3), where reports frequently use bespoke wording, hide the value in a table footnote, or report partial sub-figures that confuse the retrieval step. The same indicators also produce many \emph{wrong} extractions because firms disclose multiple consolidations (e.g., group-wide versus segment-level, with or without biogenic emissions) and the LLM occasionally selects a competing nearby figure. Conversely, employee counts, the share of female employees, and total water and land use achieve accuracies above $84\%$; these indicators are typically disclosed as a single, prominently placed number with a stable wording. The annual total remuneration ratio is the lone outlier on the low end ($46\%$): firms report this metric inconsistently, often as a derived ratio with multiple definitions, which yields a high \emph{wrong} rate that is not retrieval-bound but reflects genuine ambiguity in the underlying disclosure.


```{=latex}
\end{multicols}
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-performance
#| fig-cap: "Per-indicator extraction accuracy on the human-reviewed subset of the public release covering Euro Stoxx 50 and DAX 40 companies in reporting years 2024--2025. Bars are sorted by accuracy. Each stacked bar shows the composition of the reviewed pairs into five outcomes; the rightmost annotation reports the number of reviewed pairs $n$ and the per-indicator accuracy."
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7.8
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

import textwrap
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rows = sorted(_perf_snapshot["by_field"], key=lambda r: r.get("accuracy_pct") or 0)

def wrap(s, w=42):
    return textwrap.fill(s[:1].upper() + s[1:], width=w)

names   = [wrap(r["field_name"]) for r in rows]
correct = np.array([r["correct"] for r in rows], dtype=float)
wrong   = np.array([r["wrong"]   for r in rows], dtype=float)
fn_     = np.array([r["fn"]      for r in rows], dtype=float)
fp_     = np.array([r["fp"]      for r in rows], dtype=float)
err     = np.array([r["error"]   for r in rows], dtype=float)
denom   = np.maximum(correct + wrong + fn_ + fp_ + err, 1)
to_pct  = lambda x: 100.0 * x / denom

CLR_CORRECT = "#10B981"  # emerald-500
CLR_WRONG   = "#F59E0B"  # amber-500
CLR_FN      = "#EF4444"  # red-500
CLR_FP      = "#8B5CF6"  # violet-500
CLR_ERR     = "#CBD5E1"  # slate-300
CLR_TEXT    = "#1F2937"  # slate-800
CLR_AXIS    = "#94A3B8"  # slate-400

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "sans-serif",
    "font.size":   8,
    "axes.edgecolor": CLR_AXIS,
    "axes.labelcolor": CLR_TEXT,
    "xtick.color":    CLR_AXIS,
    "ytick.color":    CLR_TEXT,
})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 7.8))
y    = np.arange(len(rows))
left = np.zeros(len(rows))
segments = [
    ("Correct",        to_pct(correct), CLR_CORRECT),
    ("Wrong",          to_pct(wrong),   CLR_WRONG),
    ("False negative", to_pct(fn_),     CLR_FN),
    ("False positive", to_pct(fp_),     CLR_FP),
    ("Schema error",   to_pct(err),     CLR_ERR),
]
for label, vals, color in segments:
    ax.barh(y, vals, left=left, color=color, label=label,
            edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.4, height=0.78)
    left += vals

# right-side annotations: n and per-indicator accuracy
for yi, r in enumerate(rows):
    acc = r.get("accuracy_pct") or 0
    ax.text(102, yi, f"$n{{=}}{r['reviewed_total']}$   {acc:>2d}%",
            va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7.5, color=CLR_TEXT, clip_on=False)

ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(names, fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xticks([0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
ax.set_xticklabels(["0%", "25%", "50%", "75%", "100%"])
ax.set_xlabel("Share of reviewed firm-indicator-year pairs", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2)
ax.invert_yaxis()
for spine in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

ax.legend(
    loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.015),
    ncol=5, frameon=False, fontsize=7.8,
    handlelength=1.1, handleheight=0.9, columnspacing=1.2,
)

AX_LEFT, AX_RIGHT = 0.40, 0.82

fig.suptitle(
    f"Public release {RELEASE_VERSION_STR} — {PERF_TOTAL_FMT} firm-indicator-year pairs, "
    f"{PERF_ACCURACY}% overall accuracy",
    fontsize=8, color=CLR_TEXT, x=(AX_LEFT + AX_RIGHT) / 2, ha="center", y=0.985,
)

plt.subplots_adjust(left=AX_LEFT, right=AX_RIGHT, top=0.91, bottom=0.06)
plt.show()
```

# Working with the Data
All inputs underlying the figures and tables of this document are publicly available and downloaded at render time. The
following section describes how to access the data.

The extracted dataset is exposed through a small, versioned REST API at \href{https://api.srnav.com}{\texttt{api.srnav.com}}. Each *release* is an immutable, citeable snapshot of the dataset — once published, its values, version label, and row count never change; superseded releases remain reachable and any subsequent retraction is recorded on the release itself. We recommend pinning research artifacts to an explicit version (e.g. \texttt{`{python} RELEASE_VERSION_MAJOR`.`{python} RELEASE_VERSION_MINOR`}) rather than to \texttt{latest}, so that downstream results remain reproducible when new releases are published. Interactive endpoint documentation, request/response schemas, and a try-it-out console are available at \href{https://api.srnav.com}{\texttt{api.srnav.com}}, which serves a Swagger UI generated from the OpenAPI specification at \href{https://api.srnav.com/openapi.json}{\texttt{/openapi.json}}.

Access is gated by a personal API token, requested at \href{https://srnav.com}{\texttt{srnav.com}} and passed in the standard \texttt{Authorization: Bearer} header. Tokens are scoped to the issuing account and can be rotated or revoked at any time; we ask consumers to keep them out of version control and out of figure source files. The two endpoints needed for most research workflows are:

\begin{description}
\setlength{\itemsep}{1pt}
  \item[\texttt{GET /projects/\{slug\}/releases}] Lists all published releases for a public project, newest first, with publication and retraction timestamps and row counts. Used to discover the latest version programmatically and to track the dataset's revision history.
  \item[\texttt{GET /projects/\{slug\}/releases/\{version\}}] Returns the full release as JSON, where \texttt{\{version\}} accepts \texttt{latest}, \texttt{v1}, or \texttt{v2.1}. A CSV variant is available at the same path with a \texttt{.csv} suffix and produces a flattened, header-included file suitable for direct loading into a statistical package.
\end{description}

Each row of a release identifies a single firm--indicator--year observation and carries the published value together
with the firm's identifier, ISIN, country, sector, industry, and stock index membership; the indicator's slug, name,
category, unit, and data type; the year; a \texttt{source} flag (\texttt{human} for reviewer-verified values,
\texttt{ai} for AI-only extractions awaiting review); the source document identifier; and a page reference for
traceability against the original filing. A minimal request fetches the latest release:

```{=latex}
\end{multicols}
```

``` bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRN_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.srnav.com/projects/main-esrs-kpi/releases/latest"
```

The same payload is one line away from a tidy data frame in Python — the following snippet pins the request to a specific release and filters to the GHG indicators for two firms:

``` python
import os, requests, pandas as pd

VERSION = "v2.4"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SRN_TOKEN']}"}

resp = requests.get(
    f"https://api.srnav.com/projects/main-esrs-kpi/releases/{VERSION}",
    headers=headers, timeout=30,
)
resp.raise_for_status()
release = resp.json()

df = pd.DataFrame(release["values"])
df["value"] = pd.to_numeric(df["value"], errors="coerce")  # NOT_FOUND -> NaN

ghg = df[
    df["field_slug"].str.startswith("ghg_") &
    df["isin"].isin(["DE000A1EWWW0", "DE0007164600"])  # Adidas, SAP
]
print(ghg[["company_name", "year", "field_slug", "value", "unit", "source"]])
```

The CSV variant is most convenient in R, where it can be read in a single call:

``` r
library(httr2)
library(readr)

version <- "v2.4"

resp <- request(paste0("https://api.srnav.com/projects/main-esrs-kpi/releases/",
                        version, ".csv")) |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("SRN_TOKEN")) |>
  req_perform()

df <- read_csv(
  resp_body_string(resp),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character(), value = col_double()),
  na        = c("", "NA", "NOT_FOUND"),
  show_col_types = FALSE,
  guess_max = 1e5,
)
```

For programmatic discovery of the most recent published release and for any workflow that requires per-request control
(e.g. rate-limit handling or audit logging), \texttt{httr2} composes cleanly with the `releases` index:


``` r
library(httr2)

req <- request("https://api.srnav.com/projects/main-esrs-kpi/releases") |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(Sys.getenv("SRN_TOKEN")) |>
  req_user_agent("srn-research/0.1")

releases <- resp_body_json(req_perform(req))
latest   <- Filter(\(r) is.null(r$retracted_at), releases)[[1]]$version
message("Pinned to ", latest)
```

```{=latex}
\begin{multicols}{2}
```

We encourage users to cite the dataset by its release version (e.g., *Sustainability Reporting Navigator, Main ESRS KPI dataset, release `{python} RELEASE_VERSION_STR`, published `{python} RELEASE_DATE`*) and, where possible, to record the release's \texttt{published\_at} timestamp in supplementary materials so that subsequent retractions or revisions can be detected. Requests, feature suggestions, and bug reports are welcome by email at \href{mailto:hello@srnav.com}{\texttt{hello@srnav.com}}.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# Reuses `df` and `category_meta` from the "Data points" chunk above —
# same Quarto/Jupyter session, no re-fetch. Note: this prints plain
# Markdown (not raw LaTeX), so no esc() here — pandoc handles the

# Interim store for curated "Variants/Problems" notes -- not yet captured
# in schema_fields_rows.csv (manual_instructions is empty for all rows).

variants = {
    "employees_total": "Often there are different definitions of the total "
        "number of employees, especially between the financial and the "
        "sustainability report. If we find several, we choose the one "
        "reported in the sustainability report.",
    "topmgmt_female": "Different definitions of top management at firm-level.",
    "genderpaygap": "Some companies report negative gender pay gap (i.e. "
        "women earn more than man). In this case we report negative values.",
    "remunerationratio": "Different ways of reporting (e.g., 250:1, 250, "
        "25000%). In SRN Lab we would report the remuneration ratio from "
        "the example as 250.",
}

for cat in ["environmental", "governance", "social"]:
    print(f"#### {category_meta[cat]}\n")
    for _, row in df[df["category"] == cat].iterrows():
        unit = (f" *({row['unit']})*"
                if pd.notna(row["unit"]) and str(row["unit"]).strip()
                else "")
        print(f"**{row['name'].capitalize()}**{unit}\n")
        print(f"{row['description']}\n")
        note = variants.get(row["slug"])
        print(f"*Variants/Problems:* {note or '---'}\n")
```
